name: Quileute
confidence_why: The fixed penultimate coding rests on a one-word table cell in Gordon 2002, while the three first-hand descriptions disagree about what kind of system Quileute has: Andrade 1933 describes four pitch accents whose position is 'not a fixed element' and falls most often on the first or second syllable of longer words, Powell 1975 says primary stress is normally penultimate but 'not predictable', and Hoard 1993 argues that Quileute is 'simply not a stress language' and has two tones. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Gordon 2002.

sweep_summary: The single title-works with stress in the title (Baird et al. 2014b, K'ichee') is a Glottolog mis-attachment and irrelevant. this search of works with stress in the title instead recovered the catalog's missing primary: an open copy of Handbook of American Indian Languages Part 3 (archive.org tonkawaindianlan03hoij / rosettaproject_tqw_morsyn-2) containing Andrade 1933 'Quileute' with its full Accent chapter (§§26-31, pp.162-171). Andrade states that accent is not a fixed element of the word, that the primary high-tone accent in longer words is most often on the first or second syllable, and that only 'prevalent tendencies, not fixed principles' exist; the four accent types have positional restrictions only within 2-3 syllable melodic patterns (high-falling: penult only; low-tone: ultima/penult only). Google Books snippets of Powell 1975:29 (via Hoard 1993) say primary stress is 'normally on the penult' but antepenult/final stress are 'common enough so that stress is not predictable'; Hoard 1993 'Quileute tones' argues Quileute 'is simply not a stress language'. Mithun 1999:377 (held by the project): 'Stress is often but not always penultimate.' classification: the 'fixed-strict' penult coding (from Gordon 2002 / StressTyp2 bare 'Penult') is contradicted by every first-hand or near-first-hand statement located; recommend reclassification as lexical/unpredictable with a penultimate tendency (or tonal), with Andrade 1933 §§30-31 as the deciding quote. Still unobtained (priority high): Powell & Woodruff 1976 Quileute Dictionary (JONA Memoir 3, digital by request only), Powell 1975 Proto-Chimakuan pp.29-31 (UH WPL 7(2), not in ScholarSpace), Hoard 1993 (UMOPL 10, print), Hoard 1975 ICSNL 'Stress and syllable strengthening in Quileute'. Google Books page views, HathiTrust and Smithsonian repository could not be reached by automated download; the archive.org full-text API (be-api.us.archive.org/fts) and the Google Books feeds API worked.

Positional statements for short words: §27 p.165 (high-falling accent only on a penult before a short unstressed ultima), §28 p.166 (low-tone accent only on ultima or penult, never initial), §29 p.167 (middle- and high-tone accents in practically all positions).
new_statements.reading: First-hand and explicit: Andrade denies any fixed placement. Accent (a stress with one of four pitch/length profiles) is a property of the assembled word, not of morphemes; in di- and trisyllables the position is fixed only per melodic pattern (high-falling only on the penult, low-tone only on ultima/penult, the other two anywhere), and in words of more than three syllables the primary (high-tone) accent is most often on the first or second syllable, i.e. not the penult. Certain suffixes carry a fixed accent; otherwise only 'prevalent tendencies'. This is the accent chapter the catalog could not reach (it holds only a p.282 footnote plus the bare 'Penult' of Gordon 2002 / the StressTyp2 entry for this language). Read together with the snippets of Powell 1975:29 (as quoted in Hoard 1993: 'normally on the penult.. antepenult or ultimate are common enough so that stress is not predictable') and Hoard 1993 ('simply not a stress language'), the primary literature does not support 'fixed-strict penult'; the defensible codings are lexical/unpredictable with a penultimate tendency (Powell), or a pitch/tone system (Andrade, Hoard).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog (StressTyp2) codes Quileute as fixed penultimate stress. Hoard 1993 says Quileute is 'simply not a stress language' (a tone/pitch system), and even the stress analysis he cites (Powell 1975:29) says penult is only the normal position, with antepenult and ultima common enough that stress is unpredictable. It is compatible with the existing Andrade 1933 statement already held by the project (accent not a fixed element; pitch-profiled accents), which Hoard reanalyses as two tones (H, L).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Hoard's own position: Quileute is not a stress language at all; there is no culminative word-level or phrase-level stress, and no contrastive or pragmatic stress; the prominence pattern is one of pitch/tone (his 1978 AAA abstract for the same title, snippet in qOW0AAAAIAAJ: 'Quileute.. has two distinct tones - high and low', reanalysing Andrade's four accents, with the high-falling accent as a high tone on the first mora of a long vowel). He quotes the opposing view of Powell 1975:29 that Quileute has stress, 'once per full word, normally on the penult', but with antepenult/ultimate stress 'common enough so that stress is not predictable'. Section 4 (p. 420ff.) presents pitch patterns; its content is not visible in snippets.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only in the Powell 1975 passage Hoard quotes ('two degrees of stress: primary and secondary'); Hoard himself denies stress is culminative at either word or phrase level, so no secondary stress in his analysis.
new_statements.exceptions: In the quoted Powell 1975:29 passage: forms with stress on the antepenult or the ultima are common enough that stress is not predictable. Hoard reports (§3) that Andrade's high-tone/mid-tone distinction 'is open to question' (167) and that Andrade 'also postulated independent stresses, both primary and..' (snippet cut).
new_statements.identity_note: No dialect named in the visible snippets; Quileute is a single-variety language (La Push, Washington). Hoard's speaker(s) are not identifiable from the snippets. Hoard's 1978 AAA abstract and the 1993 chapter carry the same title and thesis.

readall_conflicts: The three first-hand analyses disagree on the type of the system, and none supports the catalog's fixed: penultimate syllable coding. Andrade 1933 (already held by the project, read in full in an earlier reading) describes four tonal accents whose position 'is not a fixed element', most often on the first or second syllable in longer words. Powell 1975:29 (known only as quoted by Hoard 1993 and via snippets) treats Quileute as a stress language with primary stress 'normally on the penult' but not predictable (antepenult and ultima common). Hoard 1993 (snippets only) rejects both stress analyses: 'Quileute is simply not a stress language, and stress is not culminative on either the word level or the phrase level', and (per his 1978 abstract of the same paper) posits two tones, high and low, reanalysing Andrade's four accents. The StressTyp2 'penult' entry appears to derive from Powell's 'normally on the penult' with the 'not predictable' qualification dropped. The catalog codes Quileute as fixed-strict penultimate stress (the StressTyp2 entry for this language, Gordon 2002 'Penult', no prose). Everything reachable of Hoard 1993 (snippets, pp. 417-420) contradicts that: Hoard holds Quileute is 'simply not a stress language' but a two-tone pitch system, and the stress analysis he quotes (Powell 1975:29) has penult only as the normal position with antepenult and final stress common enough to be unpredictable; Andrade 1933 (held by the project, read in full) likewise denies fixed…

sources.quote: There are four kinds of accentual phenomena in Quileute: a stress accent, for which we use the acute accent mark after the accented vowel (a', e'); a high-pitch accent indicated by the acute accent on the vowel (á, é); a low-pitch, for which the grave acent has been employed (à, è); and a composite high-falling tone designated by the circumflex accent (â, ô).

sources.note: In reviewing Andrade 1933, Swadesh classes Quileute as having 'a system of pitch accent of the general type of Takelma or Lithuanian, i.e., there is more than one kind of accent differentiated on the basis of pitch', and adds that 'this accent presents one of the most difficult problems of the whole language and, while the author has not worked it out..' (p. 220) - i.e. he accepts the pitch accent typology but flags Andrade's treatment of the accent as not fully worked out; secondhand (review), predates Powell's stress reanalysis and Hoard's two-tone analysis.
